k1.question: APP - a folder for one big customer goal, written in plain words ('Fix dispatch operations'). It holds the processes we map for that goal, and exactly one person on the customer side is its main stakeholder - the approver. You used the word naturally in round 1.

k2.question: PROCESS and STEP - a Process is one workflow inside an App ('Schedule workshop jobs'): it has a trigger (what kicks it off), a definition of done (how we know it finished), and a department. A Step is one action inside a process, done by a person, an automation, or an AI agent. A step can depend on other steps: this one cannot start until that one is done.

k3.question: TICKET - a request a client files in the portal ('this broke', 'please add X'). Staff look at each ticket and may split it into one or more internal work items. Tickets are what clients ask; work items are what we do.

k4.question: STORY - the spec doc's word for one unit of internal delivery work (a build, a fix, an enhancement, or support work) that staff execute and log time against. This is the word that confused you in round 1 - so name it yourself. Same concept, your word:

k5.question: TASK - the spec keeps a second, smaller list next to the delivery work: little admin items ('send onboarding email', 'chase the logo file') that are not client deliverables. Keep Tasks as a separate thing, or merge everything into one list with a type label?
k5.notes: I don't know what delivery work means, but a task is essentially just like a story, but related to all internal admin-related things: essentially any build, fix, to-do, enhancement, or support work that is for the company itself, like the agency itself, and nothing to do with clients or their projects, like filing taxes or getting audited or paying for a subscription or whatever. Similarly, when we talk about this for the clients, they would be called to-dos.

k6.question: SPRINT and PHASE - a Sprint is a committed block of delivery weeks for one customer, one of three kinds: planning (figuring out), implementation (building), iteration (adjusting after feedback). It carries a checklist of what was promised. A Phase is a smaller stage inside delivery (diagnostic, implementation, validation, refinement, training, enhancement); closing a phase requires all its work resolved, and moving a phase deadline asks the client to approve. Two layers - or is Phase bureaucracy?

k7.question: ENGAGEMENT - the commercial wrapper we sell a customer: blueprint (paid diagnostic and mapping), sprint (an implementation block), support (retainer), hourly (ad-hoc). Every logged minute of work points at one engagement, so money reports stay clean. Short references like BERG-SPR03 name them.
k7.notes: Keep the engagement as defined, but also engagement types can change. I don't know. We should just have this be expensive, like I can add or edit engagement types.

k8.question: SAGA - you asked twice, so here it is in plain words. When something important happens (say, the last work item of a ticket closes), two kinds of things follow. Database changes happen instantly and all-together - if any part fails, none of it happens (no half-updated data, ever). Outside-world side effects (update the Drive doc, send the email, sync the calendar) run as BACKGROUND JOBS: queued, retried automatically until they succeed, never able to block or corrupt the database part. You get a jobs screen showing every job, its status, retries and errors. I will stop saying saga and say background jobs.
k8.notes:
Why can't all of the drive, doc, email, and calendar sync also run instantly? If they can't, then it's fine. I'm okay with background jobs. Kill this SAGA word. I hate it.

Also, there is no such thing as work items. There are tickets, and tickets to be resolved can either be resolved directly, or we create stories that are assigned to the developers in the team. There are no work items, right? There are stories, and stories can be part of sprints, but that said, there is nothing less than stories. Each story, of course, will have a work log and an activity log, but those are not relevant. They are accessory data points.

m6.section: 2 · One team, many customers - who sees what
m6.question: Databases, plainly. You said sprints, stories and work logs should each be their OWN database. The catch: our database engine cannot join across separate databases - every screen mixing two of them (a work item plus its logged time) becomes multiple queries stitched in code, slower and more fragile. The base's actual design: everything starts in ONE database, a nightly job watches sizes, and a module MOVES OUT to its own database automatically when it grows - the plumbing exists and keeps APIs/MCP working after the move. My strong recommendation: start unified, let the sharding machinery split when size demands.

It is never possible that they can open two work log rows for the exact same story or for the exact same task for the exact same user simultaneously. Sure, they can start one, keep that one open, and then close it and start a new one for the exact same story, and it's all good. Simultaneous never makes any sense.
